en: Netti 6.
Sāsanapaṭṭhāna:
Wherein are the eighteen root-terms to be seen?
In the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*.
Therein, what is the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*?

It is the discourse pertaining to defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*), the discourse pertaining to purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*), the discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), and the discourse pertaining to those beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*).
a sutta dealing with defilement and a sutta dealing with purification; a sutta dealing with defilement and a sutta dealing with penetration;

a sutta dealing with defilement and a sutta dealing with the state of one beyond training; a sutta dealing with defilement, a sutta dealing with penetration, and a sutta dealing with the state of one beyond training;
and a sutta dealing with defilement, a sutta dealing with purification, and a sutta dealing with penetration.
There is the discourse on the side of purification, the discourse on the side of penetration,

the discourse on the side of defilement by craving, the discourse on the side of defilement by views, the discourse on the side of defilement by misconduct, the discourse on the side of cleansing from craving,
the discourse on the side of cleansing from views, and the discourse on the side of cleansing from misconduct.
In that regard, defilement is threefold:
the defilement of craving, the defilement of views, and the defilement of misconduct.
Therein, the defilement of craving is purified by serenity; that serenity is the aggregate of concentration.
Corruption by views is purified by insight; that insight is the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*).
Corruption by misconduct is purified by good conduct; that good conduct is the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).

For one established in virtue, if attachment should arise toward states of existence, then that serenity and insight become a basis for meritorious action consisting in development, which leads to rebirth therein.
These four suttas, when combined with their common counterparts, become eight; those same eight suttas, when combined with their common counterparts, become sixteen.
By means of these sixteen distinct suttas, the ninefold division of the sutta is established.
A verse should be inferred by means of a verse, and an exposition should be inferred by means of an exposition.
A sutta should be inferred by means of a sutta.
In this regard, what is a sutta dealing with defilement?
“Blinded by lust, shrouded by a net...”
Covered by the veil of craving,
bound by the fetters of negligence,
they are like fish in the mouth of a trap.
“They follow after aging and death,
like a calf following its mother while suckling.
This is a discourse pertaining to defilement.
“Monks, there are these four ways of going astray.
What are the four?
One goes astray through desire, one goes astray through hatred, one goes astray through delusion, and one goes astray through fear.”
“Monks, these are the four ways of going to ruin.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further spoke as follows:”
“Whoever transgresses the Dhamma out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—
his fame diminishes.”
“...like the moon in the dark fortnight.
This is the discourse dealing with defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*).
“Mind precedes all phenomena...”
Mind is supreme, mind-made;
if one speaks or acts with a corrupted mind, [suffering follows].
“Then suffering follows him,
as the wheel follows the hoofprint of the ox that draws the cart.
This is the discourse dealing with defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*).
When one is drowsy and a great eater,
sleeping and tossing about in bed like a great boar fattened on fodder—
“The fool enters the womb again and again.
This is the discourse dealing with defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*).
“Just as rust born of iron...”
Satisfied, it devours that very same [creature];
so too, one who conducts himself with excessive license is led by his own deeds to a state of misery.
This is a discourse pertaining to defilement:
“Just as a thief caught at the opening of a breach is slain and bound by his own deed;”
"Thus, having passed away, this generation in the world beyond is slain and bound by its own karma.
This is the discourse dealing with defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*).
“He who, seeking his own happiness,
harms with a stick beings who desire happiness— ”
When he dies, he does not obtain happiness.
This is the discourse dealing with defilement.
“If, while cows are crossing, ... [the bridge] breaks... (as in the full verse).
If the leader walks crookedly,
they all walk crookedly when the leader has gone astray.
In the same way, among human beings,
if he who is considered the best practices unrighteousness,
And so too all other people:
the entire kingdom lies in suffering if the king is unrighteous.
This is a discourse dealing with defilement:
“How difficult it is for these people to live,
that they commit evil while being attached to worldly acquisitions.”
“They go to the abode of many people,
to Avīci hell, which is bitter and terrifying.
This is the discourse dealing with defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya-sutta*).
“Fruit indeed destroys the plantain tree;
fruit destroys the bamboo and the reed;
honor destroys the base man.”
“Like a foal in a mare.
This is the discourse dealing with defilement.
“A bhikkhu who values anger and slander...”
“Respect for gain and honor does not grow in the True Dhamma, just as a rotten seed does not sprout in a fertile field.”
This is a discourse dealing with defilement.

“In this case, bhikkhus, having encompassed with my own mind the mind of a certain person whose heart is corrupted, I understand: ‘According to how this person conducts himself, the way he practices, and the path he has entered upon—if he were to pass away at this very moment, he would be deposited in hell as if carried there.’”

"And why is that? Because, monks, their mind is corrupted; and it is due to this corruption of the mind, monks, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
The Blessed One said this, and regarding this matter, it is said:
“Having known that a certain person here has a corrupted mind,
he explained this matter.”
In the presence of the monks and the Buddha—
at this very moment,
if a person were to pass away;
One would be reborn in hell,
for one's mind has become corrupted;
indeed, it is due to the corruption of the mind that...
Beings go to an evil destination;
just as one might set down a burden,
so it is with such a person.
"With the breakup of the body, the one of poor wisdom is reborn in hell.
Thus was this matter spoken by the Blessed One; so have I heard.
This is a discourse dealing with defilement:
“If you fear suffering,
if suffering is not dear to you;”
Do not perform an evil deed,
whether openly or in secret.
And if you have committed an evil deed, [do not conceal it].
Whether you will do it or are doing it,
there is no escape from suffering for you,
even by fleeing after having approached [it].
This is a discourse pertaining to defilement:
“Having acquired wealth by unrighteous means,
and both [parents] through falsehood;”
"Mine"—thus do fools imagine;
how indeed will that come to be?
Obstacles will surely arise.
What has been accumulated perishes;
they do not go to heaven when dead—
have they not already been destroyed by this much?
This is a discourse dealing with defilement:
“How does one dig one’s own grave?
How does one grow old among friends?”
How does one turn away from phenomena?
How does one not go to heaven?
Through greed, one digs one's own grave.
The greedy man perishes through his friends;
through greed he turns away from the Dhamma,
and through greed he does not go to heaven.
This is a discourse pertaining to defilement:
“The foolish, the witless, wander about with themselves as their own enemies.”
Performing an evil deed that bears bitter fruit—
that deed, once done, is not good.
"That which, having done, one regrets;
for which, weeping with a tearful face,
one experiences the result."
This is the discourse pertaining to defilement:
“The state of a recluse is difficult to perform and difficult to endure for one who is incompetent.”
For many are the obstructions therein where the fool falters;
but he who [knows] both the goal and the Dhamma...
While the Tathāgata is manifest,
the fool who harbors malice toward him has lived his life in vain.
And this, O Bhante, I deserve,
as does suffering even more wretched than this:
that toward the Tathāgatas, who are immeasurable, [I have acted thus].
“I am corrupting my mind, for I am not free from lust.
This is a discourse pertaining to defilement.
“One who is measuring the immeasurable...”
The wise man should discern anger:
he who is heedless regarding that which is immeasurable—
him I consider covered over, lacking true knowledge.
This is a discourse dealing with defilement:
“For when a man is born,
an axe is born within his mouth;”
The fool who speaks ill-spoken words cuts himself with that [speech],
for no sword, however well-sharpened, is so [dangerous].
Like the Halāhala poison;
thus does one fall through a transgression,
just as by a word ill-spoken.
This is a discourse pertaining to defilement:
"He who praises one who deserves blame,
or blames one who is worthy of praise;
He gathers misfortune with his mouth;
through that misfortune, he finds no happiness.
This misfortune is but slight, provided one is heedful.
That loss of wealth at dice—
even compared to the loss of all one's possessions, including oneself—
this alone is the greater misfortune.
Whoever harbors malice toward the Sugatas shall dwell for one hundred thousand nirabbudas,
and thirty-six plus five abbudas.
“The one who reviles noble ones goes to hell,
having directed speech and mind toward evil.
This is the discourse pertaining to defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*).
“He who is devoted to the quality of greed reviles others with his speech;
he is faithless, stingy, and ungenerous.”
He is stingy, devoted to slander,
foul-mouthed, manifestly ignoble,
a destroyer of beings, evil, and a doer of wicked deeds.
O man, you are at the end of your life, born of a lowly womb;
do not speak much here, for you are destined for hell.
You are scattering dust upon yourself to your own detriment.
"O blameless one, you reproach the evildoer;
having practiced many forms of misconduct,
you yourself shall go to the abyss for a long time."
This is the discourse pertaining to defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*).
In that regard, what is the discourse pertaining to purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*)?
“Mind precedes all phenomena...”
Mind is supreme, mind-made;
if one speaks or acts with a pure mind, [that will be for one's well-being].
"Then happiness follows him,
like a shadow that never leaves.
This is the discourse on the portion dealing with perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Mahānāma the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, this Kapilavatthu is prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and congested with traffic.
Therefore, venerable sir, whether it be after having attended upon the Blessed One or those bhikkhus who are worthy of esteem, at the time of evening..."
"Entering Kapilavatthu, venerable sir, I encountered a stray elephant, I encountered a stray horse,
I encountered a stray chariot, I encountered a stray cart, and I encountered a stray person;
at that time, venerable sir, my mindfulness directed toward the Blessed One would simply lapse."
“Mindfulness regarding the Dhamma is forgotten; mindfulness regarding the Saṅgha is forgotten.
Then, venerable sir, this thought occurs to me: ‘If I were to pass away at this late afternoon hour, what would be my destination?
What would my future state be? “Do not fear, Mahānāma! Do not fear, Mahānāma! Your death will be blameless; your passing away will be blameless.”
“Mahānāma, a noble disciple endowed with four qualities inclines toward Nibbāna, leans toward Nibbāna, and tends toward Nibbāna.
What are the four?
Here, Mahānāma, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha, [thinking]: ‘Indeed, that Blessed One is an arahant... the Buddha, the Blessed One.’”
In the Dhamma …pe… in the Saṅgha …pe… he is possessed of the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken …pe… [and so forth].
“...conducive to concentration.
Mahānāma, suppose there were a tree that sloped toward the east, slanted toward the east, and inclined toward the east; if it were cut at its root, in which direction would it fall?
“Venerable sir, it would fall in whichever direction it sloped, slanted, and inclined.”
“In the same way, Mahānāma, a noble disciple endowed with these four qualities inclines toward Nibbāna, leans toward Nibbāna, and tends toward Nibbāna.
Do not fear, Mahānāma; do not fear, Mahānāma. Your death will not be an evil one; your passing away will not be an evil one.
This is the discourse on the portion dealing with perfuming (*vāsanā*).
“He who, seeking his own happiness,
does not harm with a stick beings who also desire happiness— ”
“Having passed away, he attains happiness.
This is the discourse on the portion dealing with perfuming (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
“If, among cattle rushing forward...”
The bull goes straight;
all of them go straight when the leader has gone straight.
In the same way, among human beings,
whoever is regarded as the best—
if that person practices the Dhamma—
How much more so the rest of the people;
the entire kingdom lives in happiness if the king is righteous.
This is the discourse on the portion concerning latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were engaged in making robes for the Blessed One, thinking, "When his robes are finished, at the end of the three months, the Blessed One will set out on tour."
Now at that time, the two supervisors, Isidatta and Purāṇa, were staying at Sāketa on some business.
The two supervisors, Isidatta and Purāṇa, heard it said: "It seems many bhikkhus are making robes for the Blessed One.
When his robes are finished and the three months have passed, the Blessed One will set out on tour."

Then the superintendents Isidatta and Purāṇa stationed a man on the road, saying, "When you, good man, see the Blessed One approaching—the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—then you should inform us.

After standing there for two or three days, that man saw the Blessed One coming from afar; having seen him, he went to where the superintendents Isidatta and Purāṇa were, and having approached them, he said this to the superintendents Isidatta and Purāṇa:
“Venerable sir, here comes the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; now is the time for you to do as you think fit.
Then the overseers Isidatta and Purāṇa approached the Blessed One, and having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they followed closely behind him.
Then the Blessed One, having stepped down from the road, approached a certain tree root, and having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat.
The superintendents Isidatta and Purāṇa, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, the superintendents Isidatta and Purāṇa said this to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, whenever we hear that the Blessed One is about to set out on a wandering tour among the Kosalans from Sāvatthī, at that time we feel dissatisfaction and grief, thinking: ‘The Blessed One will be far away from us.’”

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One has set out on a wandering tour from Sāvatthī among the Kosalans, at that time there arises in us a lack of gladness and dejection, thinking: "The Blessed One is far from us.

... [as before] ... But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour from among the Kāsīs into Magadha, at that time there arises in us a lack of gladness and dejection, thinking: "The Blessed One will be far from us."

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One has set out on a wandering tour among the Kāsīs and the Magadhans, at that time there arises in us no small measure of dissatisfaction and no small measure of dejection, thinking: ‘The Blessed One is far from us.

And when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One will set out on a wandering tour among the Magadhans and the Kāsīs, at that time there arises in us a sense of gladness and joy, thinking: ‘The Blessed One will be near to us.’

But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One has set out on tour among the Magadhans or the Kāsīs, at that time there arises in us a state of gladness and joy, thinking: "The Blessed One is near to us.

... [as before] ... But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One will set out on tour from among the Kosalans toward Sāvatthī, at that time there arises in us a state of gladness and joy, thinking: "The Blessed One will soon be with us."

“But when we hear, venerable sir, that the Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, on that occasion there arises in us no small measure of gladness and no small measure of joy, thinking: ‘The Blessed One is near to us.
“Therefore, headmen, household life is confinement, a path of dust; going forth is the open air. And it is enough for you, headmen, to be diligent.”
“Venerable sir, is there for us another confinement that is more confining and more commonly regarded as a confinement than this one?
“But what, householder-officials, is that other confinement which is more confining and more commonly regarded as a confinement than this one?
“Venerable sir, it is when King Pasenadi of Kosala wishes to go out to the pleasure gardens, and those [who accompany him]...”
Those were the royal elephants of King Pasenadi of Kosala, fit for riding;
having prepared them, we had those queens of King Pasenadi of Kosala who were dear and beloved sit, one in front and one behind.
Now, venerable sir, such was the fragrance of those sisters.
It was, venerable sir, as if a casket of perfumes were being opened; it was like the fragrance of royal maidens adorned with scents.
And the touch of those sisters’ bodies, venerable sir, was such that it was like a tuft of cotton or a tuft of silk-cotton, as is the case with well-nurtured royal maidens.
At that time, venerable sir, even a nāga had to be guarded.
“Those sisters must also be guarded;
one’s own self must also be guarded.

Yet, venerable sir, we do not recall ever giving rise to an evil thought toward those sisters. Venerable sir, this is another confinement for us, more confining than that previous one, and considered even more of a confinement.”
“Therefore, householders, the life of a householder is a crowded path, a path of dust; going forth is like the open air.
It is enough for you, householders, to be diligent.

Householders, a noble disciple endowed with four qualities is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment. What are the four?”
By which four?

Here, householder-stewards, a well-taught noble disciple possesses verified confidence in the Buddha, thinking: "Thus indeed is that Blessed One: worthy, perfectly awakened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses verified confidence in the Dhamma... [and] in the Saṅgha...

With a mind free from the stain of stinginess, he dwells at home, open-handed, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to charity, accessible to requests, and rejoicing in the distribution of gifts without making distinctions.
"Householders, a noble disciple endowed with these four qualities is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment.

You, householders, are endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha, thinking: 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened... the Teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. [You are endowed] with verified confidence in the Dhamma... [and] with verified confidence in the Saṅgha..."
"Whatever gifts there may be in the family, all of them are shared without reservation with those who are virtuous and of good character.
What do you think, masters of the household: how many people are there among the Kosalans who are equal to you in this regard, namely, in giving and sharing?"
“It is a gain for us, Bhante; it is a great fortune for us, Bhante, that the Blessed One understands us in this way.
This is the discourse on the portion concerning spiritual cultivation (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
“Having offered a single flower...”
For a thousand ten-million eons,
among both gods and humans, he has lived;
by the remainder [of his merit], he has attained final Nibbāna.
This is the discourse pertaining to the stage of habituation:
“In the Assattha tree, green and shining,
with its foliage fully grown;”
I attained a single perception directed toward the Buddha while being mindful;
thirty eons from then until today—
I do not recognize any state of woe;
the three knowledges have been realized—
this is the residual impression of that perception.”
This is the discourse pertaining to the portion on latent tendencies:
“The Supreme Person entered the city of Kosala for alms;”
Compassionate before the meal,
the Sage who has destroyed craving holds a flower-earring in his hand.
Adorned with all kinds of flowers,
he beheld the Fully Enlightened One,
seated in the midst of the community of monks.
Seeing him entering by the royal road,
honored by gods and humans, he,
being joyful, gladdened his heart.
He approached the Fully Awakened One.
He [offered] that fragrant ear-ornament,
beautiful and delightful.
With his own hands, full of faith, he offered it to the Fully Enlightened One. Then,
like a crest of fire, its color—
From the Buddha’s mouth,
a flame like a thousand-rayed lightning bolt issued forth.
Having performed a circumambulation,
he placed [the bowl] three times upon his head, honoring the Kinsman of the Sun.
They vanished from sight right before my eyes.
Having seen this marvel,
this extraordinary and hair-raising wonder;
Having arranged his robe over one shoulder,
Ānanda said this:
“What is the cause for this act of shivering?”
Explain it, O Great Sage!
There will be a light of the Dhamma;
dispel our doubt, O Sage.
For one in whom that knowledge always proceeds regarding all phenomena,
[there is no doubt] for the elder who was once full of uncertainty and perplexity.
He said this to Ānanda:
"Ānanda, that man who placed his mind in confidence in me— "
For eighty-four eons,
he will not go to an evil destination;
among the gods, he will possess divine splendor.
Having ruled over divine sovereignty,
he will become a lord of men among humans—
a king over the realm.
Thus, having gone forth at the very end and realized the nature of phenomena,
he became a Paccekabuddha, free from passion.
It shall be known as the "Ear-ornament.
When the mind is full of faith,
there is no such thing as a small gift.
Whether toward the Tathāgata, the Fully Awakened One,
or toward his disciple—
thus inconceivable are the Buddhas.
“The qualities of the Buddha are inconceivable;
for those who have faith in what is inconceivable,
the result is inconceivable.”
This is the discourse concerning the portion dealing with latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).

“Here, monks, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I understand his mind as being confident. As this person conducts himself, the practice he has undertaken, and the path he has ascended—should he pass away at this very moment, he would be placed in heaven just as if he were carried there.”
"And for what reason?

Because, monks, their mind is serene; and it is because of this serenity of mind that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
The Blessed One said this, and regarding this matter, it is said:
“Having recognized that a certain person here has a mind of confidence,
he explained this matter.”
In the presence of the monks and the Buddha,
at this very moment,
a person might pass away.
One would be reborn in heaven,
for one's mind has been made serene; indeed,
it is because of the serenity of the mind.
Beings go to a happy destination;
like one who has laid down a burden,
such a person is exactly like that.
"With the breakup of the body, that wise one is reborn in heaven.
"This matter too was spoken of by the Blessed One; thus have I heard it."
This is the discourse pertaining to the stage of latent tendencies (*vāsanābhāgiya*):
“O woman, you stand having boarded a boat with a golden canopy;”
"You have entered the lotus pond and are plucking the lotus with your hand.
By what means do you possess such a complexion?"
Your majesty and splendor increase,
and whatever riches you desire arise for you.
"O deity, being asked, explain this:
of what karma is this the fruit?
That deity, with a joyful mind, [replied].
Questioned by the king of the gods,
she answered the question asked of her;
thus have I heard from Sakka.
While traveling on my journey,
having seen that delightful stupa,
I brought forth confidence in my heart toward it.
To the illustrious Kassapa,
with a mind full of serene faith, I made an offering of *paddha* flowers.
“The fruit and ripening of kamma—
such as this do those who have performed merit obtain.
This is the Sutta on the Portion Concerning Habitual Tendencies (*vāsanā*).
“Discourse on giving, discourse on virtue, discourse on heaven, discourse on merit, discourse on the ripening of merit”—
this is the discourse pertaining to the stage of perfuming (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
“Moreover, even by making offerings at mounds of earth dedicated to those who possess the ten powers, men rejoice in the heavenly realms.”
This is the discourse concerning the portion on latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
“The sons of the gods possess the color of celestial bodies;
all are of beautiful form.”
Moistening the earth with water,
build up a stupa for Kassapa.
This is the stupa of the Sugata upon the Sugata’s body.
“The Great Seers, who possess the ten powers and uphold the Dhamma—
in them these gods and humans have placed their faith;
by performing service to them, they shall be liberated from aging and death.”
This is the discourse concerning the portion on habitual tendencies:
“Exalted indeed was that which I [did] for the stupa of the Great Sage;”
I offered four blue lotuses and a garland;
thirty aeons from then until today—
I do not recognize an evil rebirth;
having honored the Stupa of the Teacher, I do not go to the states of misery.
This is the discourse pertaining to the portion on latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
“Of the World-Lord who bears the thirty-two marks, the conqueror of victory...”
For a hundred thousand aeons,
being joyful, he worshipped the stupa.
Whatever merit has been performed by me—
And by that merit, O King,
he attained splendor and ruled kingdoms,
never falling into the lower realms.
Whatever eye belongs to one who tames the untamed,
being thus directed toward the Teaching—
may all that mind of mine [be likewise].
"Attained by one whose mind is liberated, through having shaken off [defilements].
This is the discourse on the portion concerning purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
"Indeed, even with mere *sāmāka* grain and boiled rice..."
He gave an offering to a Paccekabuddha—
one whose mind was liberated, who was free from all blemish, free from taints,
dwelling in peace, and whose mind was unattached.
In that [Dhamma] I placed my confidence in the supreme Dhamma,
and in that Dhamma I fixed my mind;
may I have association with those who dwell in such a way.
And never, at any time, should you have expectations regarding existence.
It was through the ripening of that very same karma that I was reborn a thousand times among the Kurus.
Among long-lived beings who are free from possessiveness,
who attain excellence and reach the unsurpassed state—
it is through the ripening of that very same karma that I [have come to be].
A thousand times you were reborn among the Thirty-three gods,
endowed with splendor and possessing exquisite garlands, ornaments,
and ointments, having attained a most distinguished body.
Through the ripening of that very karma,
I am one whose mind is liberated, free from harshness, and without taints;
by means of these [qualities], I bear my final body.
There was a meeting with those who are beneficial and those who are harmful.
Indeed, the Tathāgata, the Conqueror, spoke this as a direct experience:
"Whatever a virtuous person desires is accomplished."
"Just as it was conceived by my mind, so has it been fulfilled;
this is my final existence. This is the discourse on the portion concerning latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
“In the thirty-first aeon, the Jina,
the unshakable Blessed One Anantadassī,
was named Sikhī; the king was his brother, Sikhiddha.”
With deep faith in the Buddha and the Dhamma,
when the Guide of the World had attained final Nibbāna,
he constructed a vast and great stupa.
A league all around the Great Seer,
the God above gods, the Supreme among men;
there a man brought an offering.
Joyfully picking a jasmine flower,
when one petal fell due to the wind,
I took it and gave it to him.
Thus she spoke to me with a mind full of faith:
"I give this flower to you alone.
Taking it, I offered it up.
Recalling the Buddha again and again,
from that time until today, for thirty kalpas,
I do not recall ever having experienced an unhappy rebirth.
"And I do not go to a state of ruin;
this is the fruit of worshipping the stupa.
This is the sutta pertaining to the portion of habitual tendencies (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
“There is a city named Kapila,
well-laid out with great thoroughfares,
teeming with people and prosperous.”
There, in that supreme city of the Pañcālas, I sold boiled rice to King Brahmadatta.
Thus I saw the Sambuddha,
Upāriṭṭha, the illustrious one;
joyful, I settled my mind in faith.
I invited the Supreme among Men,
Ariṭṭha, to a regular meal,
whatever was found in my home.
Then the month of Kattika was full,
the full-moon day having arrived;
taking a pair of new cloths, he—
I offered it to Ariṭṭha.
Knowing his mind was full of faith,
the Supreme among Men accepted it.
The compassionate one, the merciful one,
the sage who has destroyed craving—
having performed that deed for him, I...
The excellence praised by the Buddha;
having wandered through both gods and humans,
one passes away from there.
In the city of Bārāṇasī,
I was born as the only son of a wealthy merchant in a prosperous family.
And dearer than his own life;
then, having attained consciousness,
he was exhorted by a son of the gods.
Having descended from the palace,
I approached the Perfectly Enlightened One;
he taught the Dhamma to me.
Out of compassion, Gotama [taught] suffering, the origin of suffering,
and the transcendence of suffering.
The Noble Eightfold Path,
which leads to the stilling of suffering;
the Four Noble Truths—
The Sage taught the Dhamma.
Having heard his word,
I dwelt delighted in the teaching.
Day and night, unwearied, I have penetrated serenity within and without.
Those taints that existed within me—
All have been utterly cut off,
and shall never arise again.
Suffering has been brought to its end;
this body is the last;
the wandering in birth and death is over.
“There is now no further becoming.
This is the discourse pertaining to the stage of purification by confidence (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
In that regard, what is the discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*)?
“Released above, below, and everywhere,
not viewing ‘I am this’—
thus liberated, he has crossed over the flood.”
“...that which has never been crossed before, for the sake of non-renewal of existence.
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
“Ānanda, for one who is virtuous, no volition need be made [with the thought]: ‘How might remorse not arise in me?’”
It is the natural law, Ānanda, that non-regret arises in one who is virtuous.
For one who has no regret, Ānanda, there is no need for a deliberate effort to think, ‘How can joy arise in me?
It is the natural law, Ānanda, that joy arises in one who has no regret.
“Ānanda, when one is gladdened, no volition need be made for the thought, ‘May rapture arise in me.
It is the natural law, Ānanda, that rapture arises in one who is gladdened.
Ānanda, when one’s mind is rapturous, no volition need be made for the thought, ‘May my body become tranquil.’”
It is the natural law, Ānanda, that the body of one who is joyful becomes tranquil.
For one whose body is tranquil, Ānanda, no volition need be made to the effect: "How might I experience happiness?
It is the natural law, Ānanda, that one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness.
“Ānanda, one who is happy need not form the intention: ‘How might concentration arise in me?
It is the natural law, Ānanda, that concentration arises for one who is happy.
Ānanda, one who is concentrated need not form the intention: ‘How might I understand things as they truly are?’”
It is the natural law, Ānanda, that one who is concentrated should understand things as they truly are.
For one who understands things as they truly are, Ānanda, no volition need be made such as, ‘How might disenchantment arise in me?
It is the natural law, Ānanda, that one who understands things as they truly are will become disenchanted.
“Ānanda, one who is disenchanted need not form the intention: ‘How might disenchantment arise in me?
It is the natural law, Ānanda, that one who is disenchanted becomes dispassionate.
Ānanda, one who is becoming dispassionate need not form the intention: ‘How might liberation arise in me?’”
"It is the natural law, Ānanda, that one who is dispassionate becomes liberated.
Once liberated, Ānanda, no volition need be made such as, 'May knowledge and vision of liberation arise in me.
It is the natural law, Ānanda, that for one who is liberated, knowledge and vision of liberation arises."
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration:
“When phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin;”
"Then all his doubts fade away,
when he understands phenomena together with their causes.
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
“When, indeed, phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all his doubts vanish away.”
"Since you have known the destruction of conditions"—this is a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
"Why do you get angry? Do not be angry..."
“Non-anger is your boon, Tissa;
for the sake of removing anger, conceit,
and malice, Tissa, the holy life is lived.”
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration:
“When shall I see Nanda,
dwelling in the forest and wearing rag-robes?”
“Sustaining oneself on whatever is gleaned,
without regard for sensual pleasures”—
this is a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
“What, having cut what, does one sleep happily?
What, having cut what, does one not grieve?
Of what single thing, indeed, ... [is it that]?”
"O Gotama, you desire slaughter! [The Buddha replied:
"Having cut off anger, one sleeps in peace;
having cut off anger, one does not grieve."
O Brahmin, the Noble Ones praise the destruction of anger, which has poison for its root and sweetness for its tip.
"For by cutting that, one does not grieve.
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
"What, once arisen, should one slay?"
What once born does one dispel?
What indeed should the wise man abandon?
What is the blissful realization?
One should strike down anger as it arises,
dispel lust that has been born,
and the wise person should abandon ignorance.
“The realization of truth is bliss.
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration.
“Like one struck by a spear...”
As if his head were on fire,
let the mindful bhikkhu wander forth for the sake of abandoning sensual lust.
As if struck by a sword,
as if my head were on fire,
[I strive] for the abandonment of the view of a self-existent body.
“A mindful bhikkhu should wander.
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration.
“All accumulations end in exhaustion;”
All conditioned things end in fall;
for all, having encountered death, life is unstable.
Perceiving this danger in death,
one should perform meritorious deeds that bring happiness;
for all accumulations end in exhaustion.
All conditioned things end in fall;
for all, having encountered death, life is unstable.
“Perceiving this fear in death,
one who seeks peace should abandon the bait of the world.
This is the discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
“The sages sleep in happiness;
they do not grieve hereafter,
their minds delighting in meditative absorption.”
Possessed of wisdom, well-concentrated,
with energy aroused and resolute,
he crosses the flood that is so difficult to cross.
Detached from the perception of sensual desire,
having transcended all fetters,
with delight in existence completely exhausted—
“He does not sink in what is deep.
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
“Having faith in the Arahants...”
The Dhamma for the attainment of Nibbāna;
through heedfulness and discernment, one gains wisdom and the desire to hear.
One who acts appropriately, bears the burden,
and exerts effort finds wealth;
through truth, one attains fame.
Giving binds one with friends;
thus, passing from this world to the next, one does not grieve.
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration:
“For you who have abandoned all fetters and are fully liberated;”
"It is not good for a recluse when he instructs another.
In whatever way, by whatever means...
Co-residence arises, O Sakyan;
a wise person ought not to feel compassion for such a one even in their mind.
If one instructs another with a mind full of faith,
one does not become bound by that act.
“Whatever compassion and sympathy there is”—
this is a discourse pertaining to penetration.
“From what source do lust and hatred arise?”
Whence arise discontent, delight, and horripilation?
Whence do mental thoughts emerge,
like young birds darting out from a hawk?
Lust and hatred have their source here;
discontent, delight, and horripilation are born from this;
from this they arise—the mental fabrications of the mind.
Young children let go of him like a hawk;
born of affection, arisen from themselves,
like branches growing from the trunk of a banyan tree.
Attached to various sensual pleasures like a spreading creeper in the forest,
those who understand from what source this arises—
They dispel these [defilements]; listen, O Yakkha!
They cross over this flood so difficult to cross, which was never crossed before, for the sake of no further becoming.
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration:
“It is difficult, Blessed One; it is very difficult, Blessed One. “They do indeed perform what is difficult,” [said the Blessed One].
"O Kāmada," said the Blessed One,
"the trainees, established in virtue and concentration,
remain steadfast because they have entered the homeless life."
“Contentment brings happiness.
“Blessed One, this contentment is indeed difficult to find.
“They do indeed obtain that which is difficult to find.”
"Those who delight in the calming of the mind, both by day and by night," said the Blessed One, "are free from desire."
“The mind delights in meditation.
“This mind, Blessed One, is difficult to concentrate.
“Even that which is difficult to concentrate, they do concentrate.”
"Those who delight in the tranquility of the faculties, O Bhagavā,
having cut through the net of Death,"
“The Noble Ones go along, bestowing desires.
“The path, Blessed One, is difficult to traverse and uneven.
“Whether it be difficult to traverse or uneven,”
The noble ones go where they desire;
the ignoble fall headlong upon the uneven path.
"The path is equal for the noble ones,
for the noble ones are even amidst the uneven.
This is the discourse pertaining to penetration.
“This indeed is that Jeta’s Grove,
frequented by the assembly of seers;
it has been inhabited by the King of Dharma.”
It produces joy for me:
action, clear vision, and the Dhamma;
virtue is the supreme livelihood.
By this mortals are purified,
not by lineage or wealth;
therefore, a wise person—
Perceiving one's own welfare,
one should investigate the Dhamma with systematic reflection;
thus one is purified therein.
Sāriputta alone is supreme in wisdom,
in virtue, and in tranquility—
even that bhikkhu who has gone to the further shore.
“...this much may be the ultimate.
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
“One should not pursue the past...”
One should not long for the future;
for that which is past has been abandoned,
and that which is yet to come has not been reached.
And whoever discerns, here and there, the phenomenon of the present—
unshakable and unshakeable—
Knowing this, one should cultivate it.
Diligence is the duty to be done this very day;
who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For we have no compact with that Death who has a great army.
With one who dwells thus, ardent—
“Unwearied by day and night—
him indeed the peaceful Sage calls ‘One Fortunate Night.’”
This is a discourse pertaining to penetration.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four things to be realized. Which four?”
“Monks, there are phenomena to be realized through the eye and through wisdom; there are phenomena to be realized through mindfulness and through wisdom;
there are phenomena to be realized through the body and through wisdom; and there are phenomena to be known through wisdom and to be realized through wisdom.”
"And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be realized by means of the eye and by means of wisdom?
The well-purified divine eye, which surpasses the human, is to be realized by means of the eye and by means of wisdom.
And what, bhikkhus, are the things to be realized by means of mindfulness and by means of wisdom?"
The recollection of past lives is to be realized through mindfulness and wisdom.
And what, monks, are the phenomena to be realized through the body and through wisdom?
The various supernormal powers and cessation are to be realized through the body and through wisdom.
"And what, bhikkhus, are the phenomena to be known by wisdom, to be realized by wisdom?
The knowledge of the destruction of the taints is to be known by wisdom, and it is to be realized by wisdom.
This is the discourse pertaining to penetration.
In this regard, what is a discourse pertaining to the one beyond training (*asekkha*)?
“He whose mind is like a rock,
steady and unshakable;”
Detached from things that provoke lust,
not provoked by things that provoke anger—
whose mind is thus developed, [he is liberated].
“From where will suffering come to him?
This is the discourse pertaining to the one beyond training (asekkha).
And the tenth exposition concerning the wandering of the Venerable Sāriputta should be composed.
This is a discourse pertaining to those beyond training (asekkha):
“The brahmin who has banished evil states,
who is free from grunting and free from dregs, self-controlled;”
One who has mastered the Vedanta and lived the holy life may rightly proclaim the doctrine of Brahma—
one for whom there is no conceit anywhere in the world.
This is a discourse pertaining to those beyond training (asekkha).
“Having cast out evil states,
those who always live mindful;”
“The Buddhas, whose fetters are destroyed—
they indeed are the brahmins in the world.
This is the discourse concerning those beyond training (asekkha).
“Where water, earth,
fire, and air find no footing,
there the white stars do not shine.”
The sun does not shine there;
the moon does not gleam there,
nor is darkness found there.
And when the sage, through his own sagehood, has realized this as a brahmin,
then both forms and formless things—
“One is liberated from pleasure and pain.
This is a discourse concerning those beyond training (*asekkha*).
“When, regarding one’s own phenomena...”
The brahmin becomes one who has gone to the further shore;
thus he transcends both this Piśāca and the Pakkula.”
This is a discourse pertaining to one beyond training (asekkha):
“He does not rejoice in what comes,
nor does he grieve when it departs.”
“One who has abandoned all attachments, a victor in battle—
him I call a brahmin. This is the discourse concerning the one beyond training (asekkha).
“One does not become pure through water;
many people bathe here [in it].
But he in whom truth and Dhamma abide—”
“He is pure, and he is a brahmin.
This is the discourse concerning the one beyond training (asekkha).
“When phenomena indeed become manifest...”
For the brahmin who meditates with ardor,
dispelling the army of Māra,
he stands like the sun illuminating the sky.
This is a discourse concerning those beyond training (asekkha):
“Behold him with tranquil faculties, moving about,
having attained the threefold knowledge, and possessing a nature free from defilement.”
Having transcended all bonds,
possessing nothing, he fares about as a wearer of rag-robes;
many sublime deities [attend him].
Having approached the Brahma-palace,
they pay homage with serene minds to that noble steed of pure breed, possessed of natural strength and self-control.
Homage to you, O noble steed among men;
homage to you, O supreme among men;
for whom we do not fully comprehend—
“On what do you rely when you meditate?
This is a discourse concerning the one beyond training (asekkha).
“These monks are indeed companions.”
They have practiced for a long time;
their true Dhamma accords with the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha.
Well-trained by Kappina in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble One,
they bear their final body.
“Having conquered Māra and his host.
This is a discourse concerning those beyond training (*asekha*).
“This was not undertaken with laxity...”
This nibbāna, the liberation from all suffering, is not to be attained by one of little strength.
And this young bhikkhu,
this supreme person,
bears his final body.
“Having conquered Māra and his host.
This is a discourse concerning those beyond training (*asekkha*).
“Ugly in appearance, wearing coarse robes,”
Mogharāja, always mindful,
with taints destroyed, detached,
having done what was to be done, and free from outflows.
Possessing the threefold knowledge, attained to supernormal powers,
and skilled in discerning the minds of others,
he bears his final body.
“Having conquered Māra and his host.
This is a discourse concerning the one beyond training (*asekkha*).

“Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, through revulsion toward form, through its fading away, through its cessation, and through non-clinging, being liberated, is called ‘the Perfectly Enlightened One.’”
“Monks, a monk who is liberated by wisdom, through disenchantment with, dispassion toward, and the cessation of form, being liberated through non-clinging, is called ‘liberated by wisdom.
So too, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, [is liberated] through disenchantment with, dispassion toward, and the cessation of feeling … perception …”
Through disenchantment with, dispassion for, and the cessation of volitional formations... and consciousness, one who is liberated through non-clinging is called a "Perfectly Enlightened One.
Monks, a monk who is liberated by wisdom, through disenchantment with, dispassion for, and the cessation of consciousness, being liberated through non-clinging, is called "one liberated by wisdom."
"In that regard, monks, what is the distinction, what is the superiority, what is the difference between a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, and a monk liberated by wisdom?
"Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One...
[as before] "...Monks, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is the arouser of the unarisen path, the producer of the unproduced path."

“Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One is the arouser of the path, the declarer of the undeclared path, the knower of the path, the discoverer of the path, the one skilled in the path;
and his disciples now dwell following that path, having subsequently attained it.
This, bhikkhus, is the distinction, this is the excellence, this is the difference between the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and a bhikkhu liberated by wisdom.”
This is a discourse pertaining to the one beyond training (asekkha).
In this regard, what is a discourse pertaining both to defilement (saṅkilesa) and to purification through habituation (vāsanā)?
“The rain pours down upon the covered...”
The rain does not pour through what is open;
therefore, uncover what is covered,
so that the rain may not pour upon it.

“Rain does not penetrate what is covered” refers to defilement (*saṅkileso*); “it does not penetrate what is open” refers to purification (*vāsanā*); “therefore, uncover what is covered, so that it may not be rained upon” refers to both defilement and purification.
This is a discourse pertaining to defilement and purification (*saṅkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca suttaṃ*).
“Great King, these four types of persons are found existing in the world.”
Which four?
One who is in darkness and has darkness as his destination; one who is in darkness and has light as his destination; one who is in light and has darkness as his destination;

and one who is in light and has light as his destination. In this regard, the person who is in light and has darkness as his destination and the person who is in darkness and has darkness as his destination—these two persons...

The person who partakes of defilement; the person who is dark but has light as their destination; and the person who is bright and has light as their destination—these two persons partake of purification.
This is the discourse on both the partaking of defilement and the partaking of purification.
In this regard, what is a discourse that pertains both to defilement and to penetration?
“The wise do not call that a strong bond which is made of iron, wood, or rope;”
“The passion and infatuation for jeweled earrings,
and the longing for children and wives”—
this is corruption.
“The wise call this a strong bond,
which drags one down, is slack yet difficult to release;
having cut even this, they wander forth as renunciants.”
“Without longing, having abandoned sensual pleasure”—
this is penetration.
This is a discourse pertaining both to defilement and to penetration.
“Monks, whatever one intends, whatever one plans, and whatever one is under the influence of latent tendencies—this becomes an object for the persistence of consciousness.
When there is an object, there is a foundation for consciousness;
when consciousness is established and has grown, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. From the production of renewed existence in the future…”
When there is [this], then in the future birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be;
such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
But if, monks, one does not intend, and does not plan, yet still has underlying tendencies, [then suffering arises].
This becomes an object for the persistence of consciousness; when there is an object, there is a foundation for consciousness.
When consciousness is established and has grown, there is the production of renewed existence in the future.
When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there come to be birth, aging, and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair in the future. Thus, for this...
“...there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
This is corruption.
“But when, monks, one neither intends, nor plans, nor has underlying tendencies...”
This is not an object for the persistence of consciousness; when there is no object, there is no foundation for consciousness.
When consciousness is unestablished and does not grow, there is no production of renewed existence in the future.
When there is no production of renewed existence in the future, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease in the future.
"Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering"—this is penetration.
This is the discourse dealing with defilement and dealing with penetration.
In that regard, what is the discourse dealing with defilement and dealing with the state of one beyond training (asekkha)?
“Monks, the uninstructed worldling speaks of ‘the ocean, the ocean.
But in the discipline of the Noble One, monks, that is not the ocean.
That, monks, is merely a great mass of water, a great expanse of water.”
“Bhikkhus, the eye is a sea for a person, and its current consists of forms.
This is corruption.

“He who withstands that current consisting of forms, bhikkhus, is said to have crossed the sea of the eye—with its waves, whirlpools, crocodiles, and demons; he has reached the further shore and stands on firm ground as a brahmin.”
This is one beyond training.
“The ear, bhikkhus … the nose …” [and so on].
“Bhikkhus, the tongue … the body … the mind is a sea for a person; its current consists of mental phenomena.”
This is corruption.

“He who withstands that surge consisting of the Dhamma, monks, is called one who has crossed the ocean of the mind with its waves, whirlpools, crocodiles, and demons; he has reached the further shore, stands on dry land—he is a brahmin.
This is the one beyond training (asekkha).
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
“Whoever [crosses] this ocean, with its crocodiles and its demons, ...”
He has crossed over the ocean with its whirlpools, its dangers, and its fears, so difficult to cross;
having reached the end of existence and lived the holy life,
he is called one who has reached the world’s end and gone beyond.
This is one who is beyond training (*asekkha*). This is the discourse pertaining both to defilement and to those beyond training:
“Monks, there are these six hooks in the world that lead to the ruin and the affliction of living beings.”
Which six?
There are, monks, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
If a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and persists in clinging to them, this, monks, is called...
The bhikkhu has swallowed the hook of Māra; he has fallen into misfortune, he has fallen into calamity, and he is at the disposal of the Evil One as he wishes.
There are, bhikkhus, sounds cognizable by the ear...
[and so on] ...smells cognizable by the nose... [and so on].
Tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body...

mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust—if a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them;
“Monks, this is called a monk who has swallowed the hook of Māra; he has fallen into misfortune, he has fallen into calamity, and he is at the disposal of the Evil One as he wishes.
This is corruption.
And there are, monks, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, endearing, and connected with sensual desire.

If a bhikkhu does not delight in, does not welcome, and does not remain clinging to that which is delightful, then, monks, this bhikkhu is said to be one who has not swallowed Māra’s hook; he has broken the hook, shattered the hook;
he has not fallen into calamity, he has not fallen into disaster, and he is no longer subject to the will of the Evil One.
“There are, monks, sounds cognizable by the ear...
[and so on] ...mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.

If a monk does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, he is called, monks, a monk who has not swallowed Māra’s hook; he has broken the hook, shattered the hook; he has not met with misfortune, he has not met with calamity, and he is not subject to the doing as he wishes by the Evil One.”
This is the one beyond training (*asekkha*). This is the discourse pertaining to defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*) and the discourse pertaining to the one beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*).
In that regard, what is the discourse pertaining to defilement, penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), and the one beyond training?
“This world is born of anguish;
oppressed by contact, it speaks of disease as ‘self.
For whatever they conceive of, [it turns out otherwise].”
Then it becomes otherwise. The world, subject to change, attached to existence,
and overcome by existence, delights only in existence.
"What one delights in is fear;
what one fears is suffering.
This is corruption.
“Indeed, this holy life is lived for the sake of abandoning existence.
This is penetration.
“Whatever ascetics or brahmins have declared liberation from existence by means of existence, I say that they are all not liberated from existence.”
"Furthermore, whatever ascetics or brahmins have declared that escape from existence is through non-existence, I say they have all failed to escape from existence.
For it is in dependence upon acquisitions (*upadhi*) that this suffering arises.
This is corruption.
“With the destruction of all clinging, there is no arising of suffering.
This is penetration.

“Behold this world, beset by manifold ignorance; beings delight in what has come to be, not being freed from becoming—whatever states of existence there may be, in every way and in every respect, all those states of existence are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.”
This is corruption.
"One who sees this thus as it really is with right wisdom..."
Craving for existence is abandoned,
and one does not delight in non-existence;
through the total destruction of all craving—
The complete fading away and cessation [of craving] is Nibbāna.
This is penetration.
“Of that bhikkhu who has attained extinction...”
Without clinging, there is no further becoming;
Māra is overcome, the battle is won;
such a one has transcended all states of existence.
This is one who is beyond training (*asekkha*).
This is the discourse portion concerning defilement, the portion concerning penetration, and the portion concerning those beyond training:
“Bhikkhus, there are these four persons.”
“What four?
One who goes with the stream, one who goes against the stream, one who is established in himself, and the brahmin who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on firm ground.
In this context, the person who goes with the stream is the type of person who partakes in defilement.
In this regard, the person who goes against the stream and the one whose self is established—these two persons partake of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
In this regard, the person who has crossed over, gone to the further shore, and stands on dry land—the brahmin—is one beyond training (*asekkha*).
This is the discourse that partakes of defilement, partakes of penetration, and partakes of the state of one beyond training.
In this regard, what is a discourse that pertains to defilement, to purification, and to penetration?
There is a person of six castes who is black, born of a black womb, and gives birth to a black state;
there is a person who is black, born of a black womb, and gives birth to a bright state; there is a person who is black, born of a black womb... [and so forth].

One attains Nibbāna—which is neither black nor white, has neither black nor white fruition, and is seen as the ultimate—there is a person who is white, born of a white lineage, who gives birth to a black state; there is a person who is white, born of a white lineage, who gives birth to a white state;
and there is a person who is white, born of a white lineage, [who gives birth to] that which is neither black nor white, having neither black nor white fruition.
One attains Nibbāna, which is seen in its ultimate sense.

In this regard, the person who is dark, born of darkness, and produces dark qualities, and the person who is bright, born of brightness, but produces dark qualities—these two persons partake of defilement.

In this regard, the person who is dark, born of darkness, but produces bright qualities, and the person who is bright, born of brightness, and produces bright qualities—these two persons partake of purification.
In this regard, the person who is black, born of a black lineage, and who attains Nibbāna— which is seen as the ultimate, neither black nor white, and having a result that is neither black nor white—
and the person who is white, born of a white lineage, and who attains Nibbāna— which is seen as the ultimate, neither black nor white, and having a result that is neither black nor white—
these two persons partake of penetration; this [category] pertains to defilement.
The discourse on the side of spiritual cultivation and the discourse on the side of penetration:
“Monks, there are these four kinds of kamma. Which four?”
“There is black karma with black result; there is white karma with white result;

there is black-and-white karma with black-and-white result; there is karma that is neither black nor white with neither-black-nor-white result—this is the supreme karma, the best of karmas, which leads to the destruction of karma.”
In this context, that action which is dark with dark result, and that action which is dark-and-bright with dark-and-bright result—this is corruption (*saṅkileso*).
That action which is bright with bright result—this is the latent impression (*vāsanā*).
And that action which is neither dark nor bright, with neither-dark-nor-bright result—the supreme action, the best action, which leads to the destruction of action—this is penetration (*nibbedho*).
This is the discourse pertaining to defilement, pertaining to purification, and pertaining to penetration.
In that regard, what is the discourse pertaining to purification and pertaining to penetration?
“Having obtained the human state, two...”
What ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
good deeds and meritorious acts,
or the abandoning of the fetters.
“‘And having performed meritorious deeds’ refers to purification;
‘the abandoning of the fetters’ refers to penetration.
Having performed meritorious deeds...”
Those who have performed meritorious deeds go from heaven to heaven;
through the abandoning of the fetters,
they are fully liberated from aging and death.
“Having performed meritorious deeds, those who have done merit go from heaven to heaven”—this is the portion dealing with spiritual cultivation (*vāsanā*).
“Through the abandoning of the fetters, they are completely liberated from aging and death”—this is the portion dealing with penetration (*nibbedha*).
This is the discourse pertaining both to the portion of spiritual cultivation and the portion of penetration.
“Bhikkhus, there are these two kinds of striving.
What are the two?
That which consists in providing robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick among those who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness; and [the other]...”
"He relinquishes; and for those who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness, it is the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.

In this context, when one relinquishes robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick among those who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness, this is "cultivation" (*vāsanā*).

That which is the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna among those who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness—this is penetration (*nibbedha*).
This is the discourse pertaining to the side of habituation and the discourse pertaining to penetration.
Therein, the discourse pertaining to the defilement of craving should be demonstrated by way of the three types of craving alone.
[Craving] for sensual desire, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
Or else, it should be demonstrated by whichever specific object one is attached to; its detailed exposition consists of the thirty-six modes of conduct of the net of craving.
Therein, a discourse dealing with the corruption of views should be demonstrated solely through the side of views, namely, through annihilationism and eternalism.
Whatever basis one adheres to by way of a view, thinking, "This alone is the truth; all else is vain," that very thing must be demonstrated [as such].
The detailed exposition of that consists of the sixty-two types of views.
Therein, a discourse dealing with the corruption of misconduct is to be demonstrated by volition and mental action through the three types of misconduct.
By bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct—the detailed expansion of which consists of the ten unwholesome courses of action.

Therein, a discourse concerning the purification of craving should be demonstrated by means of serenity (*samatha*); a discourse concerning the purification of views should be demonstrated by means of insight (*vipassanā*); and a discourse concerning the purification of misconduct should be demonstrated by means of good conduct—namely, the three unwholesome roots.
For what reason?
For the production of saṃsāra.

When saṃsāra has thus been produced, bodily misconduct, bodily good conduct, verbal misconduct, verbal good conduct, mental misconduct, and mental good conduct—through this impure ripening of kamma, these characteristics of a fool are produced.
This is the discourse dealing with defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*).
"By means of this beautiful kamma-result, this mark of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*) is produced"—
this is the discourse dealing with purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
Therein, a discourse dealing with defilement (saṅkilesabhāgiya) should be demonstrated by way of four planes of defilement:
the plane of underlying tendencies (anusayabhūmi), the plane of manifest obsessions (pariyuṭṭhānabhūmi), the plane of fetters (saṁyojanabhūmi), and the plane of clinging (upādānabhūmi).
For one who possesses underlying tendencies, a manifest obsession arises; being obsessed, one becomes fettered; being fettered, one clings.
With clinging as condition, existence comes to be; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
All defilements are included and converge within these four planes of defilement; this is the discourse pertaining to the side of defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*).

A discourse pertaining to the side of spiritual cultivation (*vāsanābhāgiya*) should be demonstrated by means of the three kinds of good conduct; a discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) should be demonstrated by means of the four truths; a discourse pertaining to the stage of one beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*) should be demonstrated by means of three factors:
the qualities of a Buddha, the qualities of a Paccekabuddha, and the plane of a disciple.
Thus it should be demonstrated within the domain of those who meditate.
In this context, what are the eighteen root terms?
They are: the mundane and the supramundane; the mundane and the supramundane; the reference to beings and the reference to phenomena; the reference to beings and the reference to phenomena;
knowledge and the knowable; knowledge and the knowable; vision and development; vision and development.
And: one's own statement and another's statement, one's own statement and another's statement, that which is answerable and that which is not answerable,
that which is answerable and that which is not answerable, action and its result, action and its result, the wholesome and the unwholesome, the wholesome and the unwholesome,
what is permitted and what is prohibited, what is permitted and what is prohibited, and praise.
In this regard, what is mundane?
"For an evil deed that has been committed does not turn to milk immediately, like fresh milk."
"It follows the fool as he burns,
like fire covered by ashes.
This is mundane.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four ways of going to ruin...
[as before] ...his fame diminishes like the moon in the dark fortnight.
This is the mundane.
“Bhikkhus, there are these eight worldly conditions.
What eight?
Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.”
“Monks, these are the eight worldly conditions.
This is the mundane.
In this regard, what is the supramundane?
“He whose faculties have reached composure,
like well-trained horses by a charioteer—
for him who has abandoned conceit and is free from taints...”
“Even the gods envy such a one.
This refers to the supramundane.
“Monks, there are these five faculties that are supramundane.”
Which five?
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five faculties that transcend the world.”
This is supramundane.
In this context, what is both mundane and supramundane?
It is the two verses beginning: “Having attained human status, there are two things: what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.”
That which is stated here as "both good deeds and merits" and "having performed merits, those who have done merit go from heaven to heaven"—
this is mundane (*lokiya*).
That which is stated here as "the abandoning of the fetters" and "through the abandoning of the fetters, they are fully released from aging and death"— this is supramundane (*lokuttara*).
This is both mundane and supramundane.
"Bhikkhus, when there is the nutriment consciousness, there is the descent of name-and-form; when there is the descent of name-and-form, there is renewed existence;
when there is renewed existence, there is birth; when there is birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be."
"Thus there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
Just as, monks, in the case of a great tree— whatever roots go downward and whatever roots go sideways,
they all convey nourishment upward— so too, monks, that great tree, being nourished by that and sustained by that, would stand for a long time."
"In the same way, monks, when consciousness as nutriment exists, there is the descent of name-and-form...
[as before] ...in this way there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
This is the mundane.
“Bhikkhus, if there is no nutriment consisting of consciousness, there is no descent of name-and-form; if there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no future existence;
if there is no future existence, there is no birth;
if there is no birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
In this way, there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
Just as if, monks, there were a great tree, and a man were to come along carrying a spade and a basket;
he would cut that tree at its root, having cut it at the root, he would dig it up, and having dug it up, he would pull out the roots.
Even if it were only as much as a blade of fragrant grass,
one might cut that tree into pieces, having cut it into pieces, one might split it, having split it,
one might reduce it to fragments, and having reduced it to fragments, one might dry it in the wind and sun. In the wind and sun...
Having cut it down, one might burn it with fire; having burned it with fire, one might reduce it to ashes;

having reduced it to ashes, one might scatter the ashes in a great wind or carry them away in a swift-flowing river. In this way, monks, that great tree would be cut off at the root, made like the stump of a palm tree, done away with, and subject to non-arising in the future.
"In the same way, monks, when consciousness as nutriment is absent, there is no descent of name-and-form; when there is no descent of name-and-form, all [this mass of suffering ceases]...
Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
This is the supramundane.
This is both mundane and supramundane.
Therein, what is that which has beings as its reference?
"Having wandered all around the quarters with the mind..."
Nowhere can one find anyone dearer than oneself;
thus each person holds their own self dear.
Therefore, one who loves themselves should not harm another.
This is the foundation of existence:
"Whosoever has been born, or whoever shall be,
all must go forth, leaving the body behind."
“Having understood that all-knowing one, the skillful person,
ardent, should practice the holy life.
This is the section concerning beings.
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses seven qualities should not be abandoned for as long as life lasts, even if one is being separated from them, cast away, or rubbed against the throat.
What are the seven?
He is dear, pleasing, respected, and worthy of esteem; he is one who speaks and is patient with what is said; he is a speaker of profound speech and does not direct one toward what is improper.”
“Monks, by these seven [qualities]...
[they] should not be abandoned.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke as follows:
“Dear, venerable, and worthy of esteem,
one who speaks and is patient with what is spoken;”
One who speaks profound words and does not urge one toward what is improper—
that is a friend for one who desires a friend.
“...should be practiced even for as long as life lasts.
This is the formulation in terms of beings.
In this regard, what is the formulation in terms of phenomena?
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world,
and whatever heavenly bliss there is—
these do not equal even a fraction of the happiness that comes from the destruction of craving.
“They are not worth a sixteenth part of it.
This is the formulation in terms of the Dhamma.
“Extremely blissful indeed is Nibbāna...”
Taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One—
peaceful, stainless, secure—
that wherein suffering ceases.
This is the formulation in terms of phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*).
In that regard, what is the formulation in terms of beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*) and the formulation in terms of phenomena?
"Having killed mother and father..."
“Having slain two kṣatriya kings and the kingdom along with its followers”—
this is the formulation in terms of the Dhamma.
“The brahmin goes untroubled.
This is expressed in terms of beings.
This is both expressed in terms of beings and expressed in terms of phenomena.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four bases for spiritual power.
What are the four?
The basis for spiritual power endowed with concentration of will and volitional formations of striving;”
“The basis for spiritual power endowed with the volitional formations of striving, accompanied by concentration through energy … by mind … by investigation.”
This is the formulation in terms of phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*).

He absorbs the mind into the body, and he absorbs the body into the mind; having entered upon and dwelt in the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness regarding the body, this is the formulation in terms of beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*), and this is both the formulation in terms of beings and the formulation in terms of phenomena.
In this context, what is knowledge?
"That supramundane knowledge by which one is called 'Omniscient'— [that is knowledge]."
“There is no decline for him;
it proceeds at all times.
This is knowledge.
“Wisdom is indeed the best in the world,
that which leads to Nibbāna;
by means of it one understands rightly.”
"The destruction of birth and death"—
this is knowledge.
In this context, what is the knowable?
“I will proclaim peace to you,
O Dhotaka,” said the Blessed One,
“a state visible in this very life, not based on tradition.”
Having understood that, practicing with mindfulness,
one crosses over attachment to the world;
that is what I rejoice in.
The Great Seer [taught] supreme peace;
having understood this and practicing with mindfulness,
one crosses over attachment to the world.
"Whatever you perceive,
Dhota," said the Blessed One,
"above, below, across, and in between;"
"Having understood this— that 'clinging' exists in the world—
one should not create craving for becoming or non-becoming.
This is what is to be known.
“Bhikkhus, it is through not awakening to and not penetrating the Four Noble Truths that we have wandered and transmigrated for so long a time—both you and I...
But now, bhikkhus, this Noble Truth of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated; this Noble Truth of the origin of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated;
this Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated; [this Noble Truth] leading to the cessation of suffering...”
"The noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated.
Craving for existence is cut off; the conduit to existence is exhausted; there is now no further becoming.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
“Because of not seeing the four noble truths as they really are;”
For a long time,
throughout various births,
these very things have been seen.
The conduit to existence has been uprooted;
the root of suffering is cut off;
there is now no further becoming.
This is the knowable.
In this context, what is both knowledge and the knowable?
Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, mental formations are impermanent, and consciousness is impermanent.
This is to be known.
Knowing thus and seeing thus, the noble disciple sees: "Form is impermanent," he sees:
"Feeling is impermanent," he sees: "Perception is..."
"He sees that volitional formations ... consciousness are impermanent"—
this is knowledge.
"Thus one is liberated from form, liberated from feeling, liberated from perception, liberated from volitional formations, liberated from consciousness; one is liberated from suffering—so I say.
This is knowledge and the object of knowledge.
"All volitional formations are impermanent"—this is the object of knowledge.
“When one sees with wisdom”: this is knowledge.
“Then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification”: this is both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
“All conditioned phenomena are suffering”: this is the object of knowledge.
“When one sees with wisdom”: this is knowledge.
“Then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification”: this is both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
“All phenomena are non-self”: this is the object of knowledge.
“When one sees with wisdom” refers to knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
“Then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification” refers to both knowledge and the object of knowledge (*ñeyya*).
“Whatever recluses or brahmins, Soṇa, [regard] form as impermanent, suffering, and subject to change...”
They regard themselves as “I am better,” or they regard themselves as “I am equal,” or they regard themselves as “I am inferior.
What else is this but a failure to see things as they really are?
[The same applies to] impermanent feeling... [and so on].
With regard to impermanent perception...
with regard to impermanent formations...
with regard to impermanent consciousness, which is suffering and subject to change, they do not regard it as "I am better."
“They regard themselves as equal, or they regard themselves as inferior— what else is this but a failure to see things as they really are?
This is what is to be known.
