“Furthermore, Soṇa, whatever ascetics or brahmins, regarding form— which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—
do not regard it as ‘I am better,’ nor do they regard it as ‘I am equal,’ nor do they regard it as ‘I am inferior’—
what is this other than the seeing of things as they really are?
In impermanent feeling …pe… in impermanent perception … in impermanent volitional formations …
With regard to consciousness, which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,
they do not regard it as ‘I am better,’ nor do they regard it as ‘I am equal,’ nor do they regard it as ‘I am inferior.
What else is there but the seeing of things as they really are?
This is knowledge.
This is both knowledge and the object of knowledge.
In this context, what is vision?
“Those who clearly discern the Noble Truths,
so well-taught by the one of profound wisdom—
even if they should become greatly negligent— ”
“They do not take up an eighth existence”—
this is the vision.
“Just as a pillar fixed in the earth...”
Unshaken by the four winds,
such is the true person I declare,
who has seen the Noble Truths through direct penetration.
This is the vision.
“Monks, endowed with four factors of stream-entry, a noble disciple, if he so desires, may himself declare of himself:

‘I am one for whom hell is exhausted, the animal realm is exhausted, the sphere of hungry ghosts is exhausted; I am one for whom the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms are exhausted.’”
“I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment;
having wandered and transmigrated among gods and humans at most seven times, I shall make an end of suffering.
By which four?

In this case, monks, a noble disciple’s faith in the Tathāgata is settled, established, grown, rooted, and unshakable by any ascetic or brahmin, by any deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, in accordance with the Dhamma;
moreover, he has reached a conclusion regarding the Dhamma: "The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, visible here and now..."
It is timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise—namely, the crushing of intoxication...
[and so on] ...cessation, Nibbāna. Furthermore, both householders and those who have gone forth find him desirable, lovely, dear, and agreeable because of his Dhamma.
Moreover, he is endowed with virtues dear to the Noble Ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.
“Monks, a noble disciple endowed with these four factors of stream-entry may, if he so desires, declare of himself:

‘I am one for whom hell is exhausted, the animal realm is exhausted, the sphere of afflicted spirits is exhausted; I am one for whom the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the lower realms are exhausted.
I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and destined for full enlightenment.’”
“Having wandered and transmigrated among gods and humans for seven more births at most, I shall make an end of suffering.
This is vision.
In this context, what is cultivation?
“He whose faculties are fully developed,
both internally and externally throughout the entire world;
having become disillusioned with this world and the world beyond— ”
“Being developed and tamed, he awaits his time.
This is development.
“Monks, there are these four Dharma-footings.”

“What are the four? Non-covetousness is a footprint of the Dhamma; non-ill will is a footprint of the Dhamma; right mindfulness is a footprint of the Dhamma; right concentration is a footprint of the Dhamma. These, monks, are the four footprints of the Dhamma.
This is the development.
In this regard, what is both seeing and cultivation?
"One should cut off five and abandon five"—this is seeing.
"One should cultivate five further"—this is cultivation.
“The bhikkhu who has transcended the five fetters is called one who has crossed the flood. This is development.
This is both seeing and development.
“Bhikkhus, there are these three faculties.”
Which three? The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known.
And what, monks, is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
Here, monks, a monk generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the realization of the Noble Truth of Suffering that has not yet been realized.

He generates desire, exerts himself, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the realization of the noble truth of the origin of suffering that has not yet been realized; ...pe... [and] for the realization of the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; ...pe... [and] for the realization of the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
“This, monks, is the faculty of ‘I shall come to know the unknown.
This is vision.
And what, monks, is the faculty of final knowledge?”
“Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is:
‘This is the cessation of suffering’... [and] he understands as it really is: ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This, monks, is the faculty of final knowledge.”
And what, monks, is the faculty of one who has known?

Here, monks, a monk, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it; he knows: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived."
"What was to be done has been done; there is nothing further for this state of being"—thus one understands.
This, monks, is the faculty of one who has realized (aññātāvindriya).
This is development (bhāvanā).
This is both seeing and cultivation.
In this regard, what is our own teaching?
"The non-doing of all evil..."
The undertaking of what is wholesome,
the complete purification of one’s own mind—
this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
This is the Master’s own statement:
“Monks, there are these three characteristics of a fool, marks of a fool, and behaviors of a fool, by which others recognize a fool as a fool.
What are the three?”
“Monks, a fool is one who thinks ill-thought thoughts, speaks ill-spoken words, and performs ill-done deeds.
These, monks, are the three characteristics of a fool, the three signs of a fool, the three manifestations of a fool.
There are, monks, these three characteristics of a wise person, the three signs of a wise person, the three manifestations of a wise person, by which others recognize a wise person as ‘wise.’”
“What three?
A wise person, monks, is one who thinks well-thought thoughts, speaks well-spoken words, and performs well-done deeds.
These, monks, are the three characteristics of a wise person, the marks of a wise person, and the attributes of a wise person.”
This is our own statement.
In this regard, what is the opponent’s statement?
“There is nothing as vast as the earth;”
No abyss is found equal to a bad person;
there is no one so lofty as Mount Meru;
there is no man equal to a wheel-turning monarch.
This is the opponent’s statement:
“Let there be victory through well-spoken words, O Lord of the Devas!
Let there be victory through well-spoken words, Vepacitti!”
“Speak a verse, Vepacitti!
Then, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, recited this verse:
“Fools would become even more enraged.”
"And there would be no one to restrain him;
therefore, the wise man should restrain the fool with severe punishment."
“Monks, when the verse had been spoken by Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, the asuras applauded and the devas became silent.
Then, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, said this to Sakka, the lord of the devas:
‘Speak, lord of the devas, a verse.’”
When this was said, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, recited this verse:
‘I consider this alone to be the restraint of a fool:’
"Having recognized that another is provoked,
he who remains composed through mindfulness.
When this verse was spoken, monks, by Sakka, lord of the devas, the devas rejoiced, while the asuras fell silent.
Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to Vepacitti, lord of the asuras:
“Speak a verse, Vepacitti.
When this was said, monks, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, recited this verse:
"O Vāsava, I see this very thing as a fault in forbearance:
when a fool considers it thus,"
Out of fear he endures this;
the fool mounts [the chariot],
like a cow fleeing even further.
“Monks, when the verse had been spoken by Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, the asuras applauded and the devas became silent.
Then Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, said this to Sakka, lord of the devas:
‘Speak a verse, lord of the devas.’”
When this was said, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, recited these verses:
“Whether he thinks so or not,
he endures me out of fear.”
The highest good among all goods is one's own welfare;
there is nothing superior to patience.
Indeed, he who is strong...

but for the strong man who is guarded by the Dhamma—
There is no retaliation [equal to it].

he acts for the benefit of both.
Both for oneself and for another;
he who, knowing another is provoked,
remains calm and mindful.
While both are seeking healing—
for themselves and for another—
people think, "He is a fool."
"Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma.
Now, monks, when these verses had been spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas, the devas rejoiced, while the asuras became silent.
This is the speech of another.
In this regard, what is our own teaching and the teaching of others?
That which has been attained and that which is to be attained—both of these are strewn with dust for one who trains like a sick man.
Furthermore, those for whom the essence is training—namely, virtue, vows, livelihood, and the holy life—and those for whom the essence is attendance; this is one extreme.
And those who speak thus and hold such a view as, "There is no fault in sensual pleasures"—this is the second extreme.
Thus, both these extremes increase the cemetery; they increase views that lead to the cemetery.
Not having directly known these two extremes, some hang back while others run too far ahead.
This is the opponent's statement:
"But as for those who, having directly known both extremes, did not exist therein, nor conceive themselves through that—there is no cycle of existence to be designated for them.
This is our own statement.
This is an inspired utterance (udāna) consisting of both the Master’s own words and the words of another.
King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
"Here, venerable sir, while I was alone in seclusion, a reflection arose in my mind: 'For whom, indeed, is one's own self dear? For whom is one's own self not dear?'"
Then, venerable sir, it occurred to me:
"Whoever engages in misconduct by way of body, misconduct by way of speech, or misconduct by way of mind, to them their own self is not dear.
Even though they might say, 'Our self is dear,' nevertheless, their own self is not dear to them."
For what reason?
Whatever a person who is disliked might do to one who is disliked, they themselves do that very thing to themselves; therefore, the self is disliked by them.
But whoever practices good conduct with the body, good conduct with speech, and good conduct with the mind—for them, the self is dear.
Even though they might say, "The self is not dear to us," nevertheless, the self is dear to them.
And why is that? Because one would do what is dear for the sake of what is dear.
They do that to themselves by themselves;
therefore, the self is dear to them.
“It is so, Great King, it is so, Great King! For whoever, Great King, engages in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, or misconduct by mind, the self is not dear to them.”
Even though they might say, “The self is dear to us,” nevertheless, the self is not dear to them.
Why is that? Because, Great King, whatever one would do to someone who is not dear, that very thing they do to themselves; therefore, the self is not dear to them.
But as for those, O Great King, who practice good conduct with the body, good conduct with speech, and good conduct with the mind, their own self is dear to them.
Even if they were to say, "Our self is not dear," nevertheless, their self is dear. And why is that?
"For whatever one dear to oneself would do for what is dear, great king, they do that very thing to themselves; therefore, the self is dear to them.
Thus spoke the Blessed One... [as before] ...the Teacher.
“If one should know oneself as dear,
one should not yoke it to evil;
for that is not easily obtained.”
There is no happiness for one who has committed evil deeds when seized by the Ender,
as he abandons his human existence.
For what does one have that is truly one's own?
And what does one take when departing?
What is it that follows after one?
Like a shadow that never departs,
both merit and evil that a mortal performs here [follow him].
For that indeed belongs to him;
taking that with him, he goes;
that alone is his follower.
Like a shadow that never departs.
Therefore, one should do what is wholesome,
as a store for the world beyond.
“Meritorious deeds are the foundation for living beings in the world beyond.
This is the discourse spoken by another.
The *anugīti* is one’s own statement.
This [verse] is both one’s own statement and another’s statement.
In that regard, what is the response?

When a question is asked, one should provide an answer such as this: "This is to be directly known; this is to be fully understood; this is to be abandoned; this is to be developed; this is to be realized. These phenomena, when grasped in this way, produce this fruit.
One should explain that "this is the meaning" for those things thus grasped.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "The Buddha, the Blessed One, is sublime," one should categorically point out the sublimity of the Buddha, the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma, and the excellent practice of the Saṅgha.
“One should categorically define: ‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,’ ‘All conditioned phenomena are suffering,’ and ‘All phenomena are non-self,’ or whatever else is of this same nature.
This is what must be answered.”
In this regard, what is the unanswerable?
"O Charioteer of men to be tamed,
may gods and humans obtain whatever they have conceived in their minds."
"One cannot know all living beings in their entirety,
even while practicing peaceful concentration free from conflict;
what does the Blessed One desire?"
This is unanswerable.

To what extent [does the Blessed One possess] the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; his deportment, his majesty, his desire for welfare, his compassion, and his supernormal power—this is unanswerable.

“Bhikkhus, with the arising of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, there is the arising of three jewels: the jewel of the Buddha, the jewel of the Dhamma, and the jewel of the Saṅgha.
What is the measure of these three jewels?
This is not to be answered.
The domain of a Buddha is unfathomable.
The discernment of the relative superiority and inferiority of individuals is unfathomable.
“Monks, the prior limit of beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving is not known,” [it was said].
“Once in hell, once in the animal realm, once in the sphere of hungry ghosts, once in the realm of asuras, once among the gods, and once among humans—I have wandered and transmigrated thus.
“What is the prior limit? This is not to be answered.
"It is not discerned" means that it is not discerned due to the deficiency of knowledge in the disciples.
The teaching of the Blessed Buddhas is twofold: that which refers to oneself and that which refers to others.
"It is not discerned" refers to that which refers to others.
“There is nothing that the Blessed Buddhas do not know” is a statement referring to oneself.
For example, concerning the bhikkhu Kokālika, the Blessed One said to a certain bhikkhu:
“Just as, bhikkhu, a Kosalan cartload of sesame seeds weighing twenty khāris…” [and so on].
But one Abbuda hell is not like that at all.
Bhikkhu, just as twenty Abbuda hells are equal to one Nirabbuda hell;
and just as twenty Nirabbuda hells are equal to one Ababa hell.
Just as, monk, twenty Ababa hells are equal to one Aṭaṭa hell;
just as, monk, twenty Aṭaṭa hells are equal to one Ahaha hell;
just as, monk, twenty Ahaha hells are equal to one Kumuda hell.
Just as, monk, twenty *kumuda* hells make one *sogandhika* hell;
just as twenty *sogandhika* hells make one *uppala* hell;
just as twenty *uppala* hells make one *puṇḍarīka* hell.
“Just as, bhikkhu, there are twenty Puṇḍarīka hells, so too is there one Paduma hell.
And it was into the Paduma hell, bhikkhu, that the bhikkhu Kokāliya was reborn after harboring a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Or whatever else the Blessed One has said—
“This is immeasurable, incalculable.
All of that is unanswerable.
This is unanswerable.
In this regard, what is both answerable and not answerable? When that Ājīvaka Upaka said to the Blessed One, “Where are you going, friend Gotama?
the Blessed One replied:
“I shall go to Bārāṇasī; I,
that drum of the Deathless,
will set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma.”
“...unconquerable in the world.
Upaka the Ājīvaka said:
“Friend Gotama, do you claim to be a ‘Conqueror’?”
The Blessed One said:
“Those who have attained the destruction of the taints are indeed victors like me.”
“Evil states have been conquered by me;
therefore, O Upaka, I am a conqueror.
Thus should it be answered as to how he is a conqueror and by what means he is a conqueror.
"What is a Victor? is not to be answered.
"What is the destruction of the taints?"—namely, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—is to be answered.
"How much is the destruction of the taints? is not to be answered.
This is both answerable and unanswerable.
"Does the Tathāgata exist? is answerable.
"Does form exist? is answerable.
“The Tathāgata is form” is not to be answered.
“The Tathāgata possesses form” is not to be answered.
“The Tathāgata is in form” is not to be answered.
"Form is the Tathāgata"—this is not to be answered.
Likewise, "there is feeling," ... pe ...
"there is perception."

"Are volitional formations [the Tathāgata]? ... "Is consciousness the Tathāgata?"—this is not to be answered. "Does consciousness exist?"—this is to be answered. "Is consciousness the Tathāgata?"—this is not to be answered.
"Does the Tathāgata possess consciousness? is unanswerable.
"Is the Tathāgata in consciousness? is unanswerable.
"Is consciousness in the Tathāgata? is unanswerable.
"Is the Tathāgata apart from form?"—this is unanswerable.
"Apart from feeling... ... "...apart from perception... [and so on].
"Is the Tathāgata [identical to] volitional formations ... or consciousness?"—this is unanswerable.
"This Tathāgata is formless ..."
...without feeling ...
without perception ...
without volitional formations ...
"Without consciousness" means it is not to be answered.
This is both that which is answerable and that which is not answerable.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One sees beings passing away and being reborn; thus all this... [and so forth].
"He understands beings according to their kamma" is answerable.
"Which beings? Which Tathāgata? is unanswerable.
This is both the answerable and the unanswerable.
"Does the Tathāgata exist? is a question to be answered.
"Does the Tathāgata exist after death? is not a question to be answered.
This is both that which is to be answered and that which is not to be answered.
In this regard, what is action?
“For one seized by the Ender,
abandoning human existence;”
For what belongs to him?
And what does he take with him when he goes?
What is it that follows after him?
Like a shadow that never departs,
both merit and evil that a mortal performs here [follow him].
For that indeed belongs to him;
taking that with him, he goes;
that alone follows after him.
“...like a shadow that never departs.
This is action (*kamma*).
“Furthermore, monks, when a fool has mounted a stool, or mounted a couch, or [is on] the ground...”
Whatever evil deeds he previously committed— misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, or misconduct by mind—
at that time they hang over him, hang down upon him, and hang all around him. Just as, monks,
the shadows of great mountain peaks in the evening time hang over the earth, hang down upon it, and hang all around it.
In the same way, monks, when a fool has ascended onto a chair, or onto a bed, or is lying on the bare ground,
those evil deeds he previously committed— misconduct by body, misconduct by speech,
and misconduct by mind— hang over him at that time, hang down upon him, and dangle all around him.
In this regard, monks, it occurs to the fool thus: "Alas, I have not done what is beautiful; I have not done what is wholesome; I have not done that which provides protection from fear.
I have done evil; I have done cruel deeds; I have done sinful acts.

To whatever destination belongs those who have not done what is beautiful, who have not done what is wholesome, who have not done that which provides protection from fear, but who have done evil, done cruel deeds, and done sinful acts—to that destination I shall go after passing away."
‘I am going,’ he grieves, becomes weary, laments, beats his breast,
and falls into confusion. Furthermore, monks, when a wise person has ascended to a chair, ascended to a bed, or is lying on the ground,
those wholesome deeds previously performed by him— well-conducted actions of body and well-conducted actions of speech— [come to mind].
The good deeds performed by him with the mind hang upon him at that time, hang down over him, and hang all around him. Just as, monks,
the shadows of great mountain peaks hang upon the earth, hang down over it, and hang all around it in the evening, even so, monks,
when a wise person has ascended a chair, or ascended a couch, or is on the ground—

When he is lying down, those wholesome deeds he previously performed—well-conducted actions by body, well-conducted actions by speech, and well-conducted actions by mind—hang over him at that time, hang down toward him, and lean over him.
In this regard, monks, it occurs to the wise person: "Indeed, I have not done evil; I have not done what is cruel; I have not done what is wicked."

‘What was well done, what was wholesome, what was a refuge for those in fear has been done; to whatever destination belongs those who have not committed evil, who have not acted with cruelty, who have not committed misdeeds, but who have done what is good, what is wholesome, and what is a refuge for those in fear—
to that destination I go after passing away,’ he does not grieve, he does not waste away, he does not lament, he does not beat his breast, and he does not fall into confusion.
When one has committed [an action], no remorse arises, thinking: "Merit has been done by me, evil has not been done;

whatever destination awaits one who has not done evil, who has not done what is cruel, who has not done what is wicked, but has done merit, what is wholesome, and what provides a refuge from fear—that destination I shall experience after passing away."
“Monks, for a woman or a man, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, I say that if they are without remorse, their death will be auspicious and their passing away will be auspicious.
This is action (*kamma*).
“Monks, there are these three types of misconduct (*duccarita*).”
Which three? Misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
These, monks, are the three kinds of misconduct.
There are, monks, these three kinds of good conduct.
Which three?
Good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind.
These, monks, are the three kinds of good conduct.
This is action.
In this context, what is result?
"It is a gain for you, monks; it is a great acquisition for you, monks; you have obtained the opportune moment, monks, for living the holy life."
“Monks, I have seen the hells called ‘Consisting of the Six Bases of Contact.
There, whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only an undesirable form, not a desirable form;
one sees only an unpleasing form, not a pleasing form.”
He sees only unattractive forms, not attractive forms.
Whatever sound he hears with the ear...
[and so on] ...with the nose...
With the tongue...
with the body...
whatever mental phenomenon one cognizes with the mind, one cognizes only an unwholesome phenomenon, not a wholesome phenomenon.
One perceives only what is unattractive, not what is attractive;
one perceives only what is disagreeable, not what is agreeable.
It is a gain for you, monks, it is well-acquired by you, monks, that you have obtained the opportunity to live the holy life.
“Bhikkhus, I have seen heavenly realms called ‘the six bases of contact.
There, whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only a desirable form, not an undesirable form;
one sees only a pleasing form, not a displeasing form.”
He sees only an unpleasing form, not a pleasing form.
Whatever sound he hears with the ear...
[and so on] ...with the nose...
With the tongue...
with the body...
with the mind one cognizes a mental object; one cognizes only a desirable mental object, not an undesirable one.
One understands only what is unwholesome, not what is wholesome;
one understands only what is agreeable, not what is disagreeable.
“It is a gain for you, bhikkhus! It is well-gained by you, bhikkhus! You have obtained a timely opportunity, bhikkhus, for living the holy life.”
This is the result:
"For sixty thousand years,
in their entirety;”
For those being cooked in hell, when will there be an end? There is no end;
how could there be an end?
No end can be seen; for then,
O dear ones, evil was committed by both you and me.
This is the result.
In this context, what is both action and its result?
"For a man who lives unrighteously and is heedless..."
Whichever miserable destination one goes to,
that unrighteousness one has practiced destroys him,
like a black snake caught by oneself.
For neither Dhamma nor non-Dhamma have equal results;
non-Dhamma leads to hell.
“Dhamma leads one to a happy destination.
This refers to both karma and its result.
“Monks, do not fear meritorious deeds; for ‘meritorious deeds’ is a designation, monks, for happiness—something desirable, lovely, dear, and agreeable.”
Moreover, monks, I recall experiencing for a long time the desirable, pleasing, beloved, and agreeable result of merits performed:
having developed a mind of loving-kindness for seven years, I did not return to this world for seven aeons of dissolution and evolution.
“Monks, when the aeon was contracting, I indeed went to the Ābhassara realm.
When the aeon was expanding, I was reborn in an empty Brahmā palace.
There, monks, I was Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power.”
Moreover, monks, thirty-six times I was Sakka, lord of the devas; many hundreds of times I was a wheel-turning monarch,
righteous, a king of Dharma, conqueror of the four quarters, stabilizer of the land,
possessor of the seven treasures— not to mention regional kingship.
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
‘Of what deed of mine is this the fruit? Of what deed is this the ripening, that I am now so powerful and so majestic?
Then, monks, this occurred to me:
“This is the fruit of three actions, the result of three actions,
by which I am now so powerful and so majestic. Namely:
“Of giving, self-control, and restraint.
In this context, that which is giving, self-control, and restraint is action (*kamma*).
That result experienced as conditioned by those factors is ripening (*vipāka*).
Likewise, the *Cūḷakammavibhaṅga* (The Shorter Exposition of Kamma) should be recited,
as it was taught to the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya. In that [text],
those phenomena which lead to short life or long life, to much illness or little illness, and to little influence or great influence—

That which leads to being ugly or beautiful, to being born into a low family or a high family, to having little wealth or great wealth, and to being lacking in wisdom or possessing wisdom—this is karma.
That which therein leads to a short life or a long life... [and so forth].
Lack of wisdom and possession of wisdom: this is the result.
This is both action and its result.
In this context, what is wholesome?
“Guarded in speech, well-restrained in mind,
and not performing unwholesome deeds with the body—
one should purify these three paths of action.”
One should accomplish the path proclaimed by the Seer.
This is wholesome.
"By whom, through body or speech..."
There is no misconduct in the mind;
one who is restrained in these three respects—
him I call a brahmin.
This is wholesome.
"Bhikkhus, there are these three roots of the wholesome.
Which three?
Non-greed is a root of the wholesome, non-hatred is a root of the wholesome, and non-delusion is a root of the wholesome.
These, monks, are the three roots of the wholesome.
This is the wholesome.
“Knowledge, bhikkhus, is the forerunner for the attainment of wholesome states, followed by a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing.
This is the wholesome.
In this context, what is the unwholesome?
“He for whom there is utter immorality,
like a creeper that has overgrown a sal tree—
he makes himself such.”
“Just as one wishes for it from every direction”—
this is unwholesome.
“The evil deed committed by oneself...”
The fool destroys himself, born from himself,
just as a diamond grinds a gem made of stone.
This is unwholesome.
"Having practiced the ten courses of action,
avoiding both the unwholesome and the wholesome;"
"And there is blame, O deity;
those of foolish mind are reborn in the hells.
This is unwholesome.
“Bhikkhus, there are these three unwholesome roots. Which three?
Greed as an unwholesome root, hatred as an unwholesome root, and delusion as an unwholesome root.
These, bhikkhus, are the three unwholesome roots.”
This is unwholesome.
In this regard, what is both wholesome and unwholesome?
"Whatever kind of seed one sows..."
Such is the fruit one reaps:
the doer of good receives what is good,
and the doer of evil receives what is evil.
In this context, that which is said—
"the doer of good [reaps] good"— this refers to the wholesome (*kusala*).
That which is said—
‘The doer of evil goes to evil’—this is unwholesome.
This is both wholesome and unwholesome.
‘By means of beautiful karma they go to a good destination.’
Through impure karma, one goes to the plane of misery;
but through the exhaustion of karma,
those whose minds are liberated go out like a flame when its fuel is spent.
In that context, when it is said,
"By means of beautiful karma they go to a happy destination," this refers to the wholesome.
When it is said—
“‘To a plane of misery by means of unwholesome karma’—this is unwholesome.
This is both wholesome and unwholesome.
In this regard, what is the permitted?”
“Just as a bee, without harming the color or fragrance of a flower,
departs taking its nectar;”
“Thus should a sage conduct himself in the village.
This is what is permitted.
“Monks, there are these three duties for monks.”
Which three? Here, monks,
a monk dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfected in conduct and resort,
seeing danger in even the slightest faults, training himself by undertaking the rules of training, and endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action.
He has a livelihood purified by skillfulness.

Furthermore, he is one who has aroused energy, being steadfast, firm in his exertion, and not casting off the burden for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states and for the cultivation, realization, and perfection of wholesome states.
Moreover, he is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading rightly to the destruction of suffering.
“Monks, these are the three duties to be performed by monks.
This is what was permitted.
“Monks, there are these ten things that one who has gone forth should frequently reflect upon.”
“What ten?
‘I have entered upon a change of appearance’—this should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth...
[as before] ...These, monks, are the ten things that should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth.”
This is permitted:
“Monks, there are these three things to be done.
Which three?”
“Good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct—
these, monks, are the three things that ought to be done.
This is what was permitted.
In this regard, what is prohibited?
"There is no love equal to that for a child;
there is no wealth equal to cattle."
“There is no radiance equal to the sun;
there is no body of water greater than the ocean.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
“There is no love equal to oneself,
no wealth equal to grain,
and no radiance equal to wisdom.”
“Lakes have rain as their limit.
Herein, that which was stated previously is rejected.
“Monks, there are these three things that should not be done.”
Which three?
Misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.
These, monks, are the three things that should not be done.”
This is prohibited.
In this regard, what is both permitted and prohibited?
"What is it that these many people here are afraid of?"
The path has been proclaimed as having many bases;
I ask you, Gotama of vast wisdom:
standing upon what does one not fear the world beyond?
Having rightly directed speech and mind,
and committing no evil with the body,
one may dwell in a house with abundant food and drink.
“Faithful, gentle, generous, and kind-spoken;
established in these four qualities,
one who stands firm in the Dhamma need not fear the next world.”
In this regard, that which was said—
"directing speech and mind rightly"— is permitted;
"not committing evils with the body"— this is prohibited.

“Living in a house with abundant food and drink, being faithful, gentle, sharing, and generous—one who stands firm in these four qualities, standing firm in the Dhamma, need not fear the next world. This is what is permitted.
This is both what is permitted and what is prohibited.
“Refraining from all evil,
undertaking of what is wholesome,
and the complete purification of one’s own mind— ”
“This is the teaching of the Buddhas.
In this regard, that which he said—“the non-doing of all evil”—is what is prohibited; that which he said—
“‘The undertaking of what is wholesome’—this is permitted.
This is both permitted and prohibited.
‘O Lord of Devas, I declare that bodily conduct is of two kinds: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.’”
“Lord of the Devas, I declare that verbal conduct is of two kinds: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.
Lord of the Devas, I declare that mental conduct is of two kinds...
[as before] ...Lord of the Devas, I declare that pursuit is of two kinds: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.”
“Lord of the Devas, I say that bodily conduct is of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated. Thus it was said; and with reference to what was it said?
Whatever kind of bodily conduct, when cultivated, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline—such bodily conduct should not be cultivated.

In this regard, whatever bodily conduct one should know: "By practicing this bodily conduct of mine, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase"—such bodily conduct should be practiced.
"O Lord of Devas, I say that bodily conduct is of two kinds: that which should be practiced and that which should not be practiced. It is with reference to this that it was said.
[The same applies to] verbal conduct... [and so forth].
“O Lord of Devas, I say that seeking is of two kinds: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated. So it was said; and with reference to what was this said?
Any kind of seeking that, when cultivated, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to decline—such seeking should not be cultivated.
In this regard, whatever pursuit one should know such that, "By pursuing this pursuit of mine, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase"—such a pursuit should be cultivated.
"O Lord of the Devas, I say that pursuit is twofold: that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated. It is with reference to this that it was said.
In this regard, as for what he said:
‘That which is to be cultivated’— this is permitted.
That which he said,
‘nor that which is not to be cultivated’— this is rejected.
This is what is both permitted and prohibited.
In this regard, what is praise?
"Of paths, the Eightfold is best..."
Of truths, the four are the feet;
dispassion is the best of phenomena,
and the One with Vision is the best of bipeds.
This is the praise:
“Monks, there are these three foremost things. Which three?”
"Monks, to whatever extent there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless;
whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared their foremost, their best, their most excellent;
that is to say, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One."

“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned—the fading away of lust for those phenomena is declared to be the foremost, the best, and the most excellent; that is to say, the crushing of intoxication … [and so on] … cessation, Nibbāna.
To whatever extent there are designations for Saṅghas, designations for groups, and designations for gatherings of the multitude,”
“The Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared to be the foremost, the best, the most excellent— namely,
the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals … the field of merit for the world.”
“The Teacher is supreme over the whole world,
the Dhamma is characterized by skillfulness,
and so too is the assembly of the Lion among Men.”
Those three remained behind:
the assembly of the lotus-like recluses,
the excellent Dharma honored by the wise, and [the Sangha].
The Subduer of Men, the Best of Men, and the Visionary—
these three are supreme in the world;
and the Teacher is without equal.
The entire Dhamma is free from burning,
and the Noble One is the best of assemblies;
these three indeed shall remain distinct.
The Victor named Truth is secure and all-conquering;
his Dharma is truth, and there is nothing higher than him.
The Noble Saṅgha is always honored by the wise.
These three are superior to the world.
One who sees the end of birth,
compassionate for the welfare of others, understands the single path.
By this path those of old crossed over,
and those who will cross and those who are crossing the flood do so by it.
To such a one as you, O best among gods and men—
“Beings pay homage, seeking purity. This is the praise.
In this context, the mundane discourse should be demonstrated by two types of discourses: that which pertains to defilement and that which pertains to purification.

Even a supramundane sutta is to be demonstrated by three types of suttas: those pertaining to the stage of seeing, those pertaining to the stage of development, and those pertaining to the stage of the Adept. This applies to both mundane and supramundane suttas.
In whatever sutta whichever word is found—whether it pertains to defilement or to purification—one should [determine its meaning] by that very word.

That which is to be demonstrated as mundane (*lokiya*)—whether it pertains to the stage of seeing (*dassanabhāgiya*), the stage of development (*bhāvanābhāgiya*), or the stage of the adept (*asekkhabhāgiya*)—should be demonstrated as supramundane (*lokuttara*) by whichever term is seen [in the text].
A discourse pertaining to purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*) serves to counteract a discourse pertaining to defilement (*saṅkilesabhāgiya*); a discourse pertaining to seeing serves...

The discourse pertaining to the removal of latent tendencies is for the purpose of suppressing the discourse pertaining to latent tendencies; the discourse pertaining to development is for the relinquishing of the discourse pertaining to vision;
the discourse pertaining to the one beyond training is for the relinquishing of the discourse pertaining to development;
and the discourse pertaining to the one beyond training is for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life.

A discourse on the supramundane (lokuttara) is to be demonstrated by means of twenty-six types of persons, who are to be sought through three categories of discourses: those pertaining to vision (dassanabhāgiya), those pertaining to development (bhāvanābhāgiya), and those pertaining to the one beyond training (asekkhabhāgiya).
Among these, a discourse pertaining to vision is to be demonstrated by five types of persons:

the once-returner with a single seed (ekabījī), the one who goes from family to family (kolaṅkola), the one who has seven births at most (sattakkhattuparama), the follower by faith (saddhānusārī), and the follower by Dhamma (dhammānusārī). Thus, a discourse pertaining to vision is [to be understood] by means of these.
It should be demonstrated by five persons.
A discourse pertaining to development should be demonstrated by twelve persons:

one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning, a once-returner, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning, a non-returner, and one who attains final passing away in the interval...

The discourse pertaining to development (bhāvanābhāgiya-sutta) is to be demonstrated by these twelve persons: one who attains final nibbāna in the interval, one who attains final nibbāna upon landing, one who attains final nibbāna without exertion, one who attains final nibbāna with exertion,
one who goes upstream bound for the Akaniṭṭha realm, one liberated by faith, one attained to view, and the body-witness.
A discourse pertaining to those beyond training (asekkha) should be demonstrated by means of nine types of persons:

one liberated by faith, one liberated by wisdom, one liberated by emptiness, one liberated by the signless, one liberated by the desireless, one liberated both ways, one with even-headedness, a paccekabuddha, and a perfectly enlightened buddha (sammāsambuddha).
Thus, a discourse pertaining to those beyond training should be demonstrated by these nine types of persons.
Thus, a supramundane discourse (sutta) based on the person (sattādhiṭṭhāna) is to be demonstrated by means of these twenty-six types of persons.
A mundane discourse based on the person is to be demonstrated by means of nineteen types of persons.

These are to be sought among those already demonstrated by their temperaments (carita): some are of lustful temperament (rāgacarita), some are of hateful temperament (dosacarita), and some are of deluded temperament (mohacarita).
Some are of lustful temperament and of hateful temperament; some are of lustful temperament and of deluded temperament;
some are of hateful temperament and of deluded temperament; some are of lustful, hateful, and deluded temperaments. One who stands at the gateway of lust is of lustful temperament;
one who stands at the gateway of lust is of hateful temperament; one who stands at the gateway of lust is of deluded temperament; one who stands at the gateway of lust...
There is one whose temperament is characterized by passion (*rāga*), one whose temperament is characterized by hatred (*dosa*), and one whose temperament is characterized by delusion (*moha*).

Standing at the gateway of hatred, there is one whose temperament is characterized by hatred; standing at the gateway of hatred, there is one whose temperament is characterized by delusion; standing at the gateway of hatred, there is one whose temperament is characterized by passion;

standing at the gateway of hatred, there is one whose temperament is characterized by passion, hatred, and delusion. Standing at the gateway of delusion, there is one whose temperament is characterized by delusion; standing at the gateway of delusion, there is one whose temperament is characterized by passion... [at the gateway of delusion].

One established in hatred as one of hateful temperament, and one established at the gateway of delusion as one of lustful temperament, one of hateful temperament, and one of deluded temperament—this worldly discourse, which is based on beings, is to be demonstrated by these nineteen types of persons.

The discourse pertaining to the stage of purification through habituation (vāsanābhāgiya) is to be demonstrated by those possessed of virtue; those possessed of virtue are five types of persons who possess natural virtue (*pakatisīla*).

The discourse dealing with the aspect of purification by habituation—consisting of the morality of undertaking, confidence of mind, serenity, and insight—is to be demonstrated by these five types of persons.

The supramundane discourse, which is expressed in terms of the Dhamma, is to be demonstrated by three discourses: that dealing with the aspect of seeing, that dealing with the aspect of development, and that dealing with the aspect of the one beyond training.
The mundane and the supramundane, the presentation in terms of beings and the presentation in terms of phenomena,

should be demonstrated by both. Knowledge is to be demonstrated by wisdom, by the faculty of wisdom, by the power of wisdom, by the training in higher wisdom, by the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor,
by right view, by scrutiny, by thorough scrutiny, by knowledge of phenomena, by knowledge of sequence, by knowledge of destruction, and by knowledge of non-arising.
It is to be demonstrated by means of knowledge—by the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has known;
by vision, true knowledge, enlightenment, vastness, sagacity, and wisdom—or by whatever other designation for wisdom is applicable.

The knowable is to be demonstrated, in brief, by means of the six objects of consciousness, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; inferior or superior; far or near; conditioned or unconditioned; and wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.

Knowledge and the knowable must be demonstrated by means of both. Wisdom, when it has become an object, is the knowable; whatever has become an object—whether internal or external—all that must be demonstrated by means of the conditioned and the unconditioned.

Regarding vision, development, our own position, the opponent’s position, what is answerable, what is not answerable, action, and result—in all such cases, one should demonstrate them by ascertaining how they are found according to how they are demonstrated in the Sutta.
Furthermore, whatever specific word the Blessed One speaks, all that should be retained exactly as it was taught.
The cause is twofold: namely, karma and the defilements; the origin is the defilements.
Among these, the defilements are to be demonstrated by the Discourse on the Side of Corruption (*saṅkilesabhāgiya-sutta*).
The Origin [of Suffering] is to be demonstrated by means of the Discourse on Defilement and the Discourse on Predisposition.
Therein, the wholesome is to be demonstrated by four discourses: the discourse on predisposition, the discourse on vision, the discourse on development, and the discourse on the one beyond training.
The unwholesome is to be demonstrated by the discourse on defilement.
The wholesome and the unwholesome are to be demonstrated by means of both.
That which is permitted by the Blessed One is to be demonstrated by means of what is permitted; that is fivefold: restraint, abandoning, development, realization, and conformity to what is allowable.
Whatever is seen in those various planes is to be demonstrated by means of conformity to what is allowable.
That which was rejected by the Blessed One should be demonstrated by way of the reason for its rejection.
That which was both permitted and rejected should be demonstrated by way of both.
Praise should be demonstrated by way of commendation.
Thus, it should be understood in five ways: the Blessed One’s Dhamma, the Noble Saṅgha, the noble qualities of the Dhamma, the training, and the attainment of mundane virtues.
In this way, the praise should be demonstrated in five ways.
The plane of the faculties should be demonstrated by nine terms; the plane of defilements should be demonstrated by nine terms.
Thus there are these eighteen terms: nine terms that are wholesome and nine terms that are unwholesome.
For it has been said: "Where are the eighteen root-terms to be seen? In the *Sāsanappakāsanī*.
Therefore, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said:
“By nine terms the skillful are defined,
and by nine they are joined to the unskillful side;
these indeed are the root terms.”
“There are eighteen terms.
Thus concludes the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*.
To this extent is completed the *Netti*, which was spoken by the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, approved by the Blessed One, and recited in the Root Council (*Mūlasaṅgīti*).
